Root cause: the result of offers.find was used without checking for undefined. claimFocusedOffer looks the highlighted id up in the current offers array and then reads offer.shiftId straight away. find returns undefined when nothing matches, and that is exactly what happens on a busy Sunday: the board polls, somebody else claims the highlighted shift, the offer drops out of the array while focusedOfferId still points at it, and the next Enter reads .shiftId off undefined and throws into the error boundary. On a quiet afternoon the list rarely changes underneath anyone, which is why it looked random. moveFocus was already safe - it guards its lookup with `if (next)` - so only the Enter path could crash.

Fix: guard the lookup. When the offer is gone the board now says so through the existing aria-live status line, moves the highlight to the first offer still on the board so the keyboard cursor is not pointing at a ghost, and returns without calling onClaim. No claim is sent for a shift that is not there, which was the other half of the risk.

Tests: the happy path still claims sh-3341 on Enter, and the second test re-renders the board without the highlighted offer, presses Enter, and asserts onClaim was not called and the message is announced.

Root cause: two writers, no coordination between them. Every keystroke armed a 600ms autosave through `scheduleAutosave`, and `handlePost` posted immediately without cancelling it. Fix, both in RebookingNoteDock.tsx: `cancelAutosave()` runs at the top of `handlePost`, so an armed timer never fires after a post; and a `postingRef` closes the narrower window where the timer has already fired and the request is in flight, since a ref is readable from inside the timeout without re-arming it. `postingRef` is cleared in the same `finally` that clears the posting state, so a later edit still autosaves normally.

The middle test is there to keep the fix from being a sledgehammer: an untouched note still saves its draft after 600ms. The third one covers what the desk sees, the parent gets the full body and the box empties.

The bulk bar is `fixed inset-x-0 bottom-0`, and it is rendered inside the scrolling list, which carried `will-change-transform`. `will-change` on a transformable property makes that element a containing block for any `position: fixed` descendant, exactly as an actual `transform` would. So the bar was being positioned against the scroll box rather than against the viewport: it moved with the scrolled content, and because its containing block was now inside the `overflow-y-auto` element it was clipped by it too. A short list is a scroll box the size of its contents, which is why the laptop looked right and the iPad did not.

Fix: drop `will-change-transform` from the scroll container. Nothing in that element animates - it is a plain overflow region - so the hint was buying nothing and paying for it with a containing block. Once it is gone the `fixed` bar resolves against the viewport again and ancestor overflow stops clipping it. Moving the bar out to be a sibling of the scroll region would also have worked, but it is a larger change and it is not needed once the containing block is gone.

What I actually verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean, so the file still compiles. That is all this diff can be checked by here. jsdom computes no layout, so a unit test cannot tell you which element is a containing block, and I have not run the iPad repro from the ticket - QA should re-run step 3 to close it. The chip built its classes by interpolation: `bg-${tone}-100`, `text-${tone}-800`, `bg-${tone}-600` and the dark variants, with `tone` coming out of `STATUS_TONES`. Tailwind scans source files for complete class strings, so `bg-emerald-100` never appears anywhere for it to find and none of those rules are emitted into the production stylesheet. The dev server serves a much wider set, which is exactly why it looked right there and flat in the build.

The refactor is a swap of the indirection: instead of a map of colour names glued into class strings at render, there are two maps of complete class strings, `STATUS_CHIP_CLASSES` and `STATUS_DOT_CLASSES`, keyed by the same `CleanroomStatus` union, so a missing status is a type error rather than a silently empty class. `tone` is gone; nothing in the file builds a class name any more.

The chip already carried its own words - `STATUS_TEXT` renders "Ready for entry", "Work in progress" or "Blocked, see bay log" next to the bay label - and that is untouched, so the printed bay log still distinguishes the three without colour.

Root cause: `retry` had nothing stopping a second call while the first was still open. Each tap set status to 'saving' and immediately awaited another `save(prefs)`, so three taps meant three requests in flight against the same record. `status` cannot act as the guard either - it is state, so the taps in one burst all read 'idle' before React re-renders. Whichever request the server finished last is the one that stuck, which is why the entry that survives is not always the last one tapped.

`useRetrySave` now holds an `inFlight` ref, set synchronously before the await and cleared in a `finally`, so a tap during a save is dropped and a tap after one is honoured whether it succeeded or failed.

I applied it to the wrong copy first. There are two files called retrySave.ts, one under settings/sync and one under settings/notifications, and I wrote the sync one. Grepping for callers put me straight: ChecklistPrefsPanel.tsx, which is the checklist preference save in the report, imports './retrySave' from settings/notifications, while the sync copy feeds DeckSyncPanel. The two files were byte for byte identical - same missing guard - so both now carry it, and that duplication is the next thing to remove; I did not merge them here because the two panels pass different save functions and I have not opened either panel.

Vitest: 2 passed against the notifications copy, the one the reported panel uses. Three taps in one act produce exactly one call to `save`, and a retry after a rejected attempt still goes through and lands on 'idle'.
